platforms.title: No Numbness Yet? Your Prostate May Still Be at Risk on a Bike
platforms.meta_description: NIOSH research on bicycle patrol officers found blood flow drops before numbness is even felt. What actually helps if you are not ready to swap saddles.
platforms.body_html:
No Numbness Doesn't Mean No Problem. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), part of the CDC, studied male bicycle patrol officers and found that riding on a traditional saddle reduced blood flow to the penis, and switching to a no-nose saddle restored blood flow to close to normal levels. NIOSH now recommends no-nose saddles for workers who cycle on the job specifically because of this risk to genital numbness and sexual function.

Why Blood Flow Is the Real Issue, Not Just the Numb Feeling

Sitting on a conventional saddle puts your body weight directly on the perineum — the area between the anus and the genitals, where the blood vessels and nerves that supply the penis and prostate area pass close to the skin. NIOSH's research points to something important: the vessels can be compressed and blood flow reduced before you consciously feel any numbness, which means "I don't feel anything wrong" isn't proof that nothing's being compressed. This is exactly why NIOSH's recommendation is aimed at occupational cyclists like patrol officers, who spend hours a day in the saddle — but the same mechanism applies to anyone riding regularly, just at a lower cumulative dose.

If you commute by bike or ride long distances on weekends, repeated compression for 30 minutes to an hour, several times a week over months, adds up even if any single ride feels fine at the time.

What Actually Helps If You're Not Ready to Replace the Saddle

Switching to a no-nose or cutout saddle is the most direct fix NIOSH's research supports, but if that's not an option right now, tilt the nose of your current saddle slightly downward — this alone shifts where the pressure lands. Set saddle height so your knee has a slight bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke, which spreads your weight across the pedals and handlebars instead of concentrating it on one point. On climbs or hard efforts, stand up and pedal ("dancing on the pedals") every so often to release the pressure momentarily.

If you ride long distances regularly, seriously consider a no-nose saddle. You don't need to match the hours-per-day of the police officers in NIOSH's study for the same underlying mechanism to apply — it's a matter of degree, not a different phenomenon.

None of this means you need to give up cycling. The point of NIOSH's research was to keep officers riding safely, not to discourage the activity — the fix is almost entirely about saddle shape and riding position, not about riding less. Most of these adjustments cost nothing and take a few minutes to try on your next ride.

Quick check: remember that feeling no numbness at all doesn't guarantee there is no compression happening; try tilting the saddle nose down; mix in standing pedal strokes on climbs and hard efforts; consider a no-nose saddle if you ride often. If you notice urinary discomfort or erectile changes, don't assume it's unrelated to cycling — talk to a urologist rather than waiting it out.
